# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel, 2026-11-20

## Short version

The jf2 memory allocator (our jemalloc fork) reduced 99th-percentile latency in the kestrel key-value store from 2140 to 870 microseconds. Throughput and median latency did not change measurably on the one workload tested. Memory use rose by 5.7 GB (9.3%), and the capacity team has not yet approved that increase.

## Words used here

- **jemalloc**: an open-source memory allocator library.
- **Build A**: kestrel at commit main@4f1c2aa with jemalloc 5.3.
- **Build B**: the same commit with jf2 in place of jemalloc 5.3.
- **ycsb-b**: workload B of YCSB (Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark). The standard mix is 95% reads and 5% updates [Ref4].
- **ycsb-a**: the write-heavy YCSB workload. The standard mix is 50% reads and 50% updates [Ref4].
- **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **us**: microseconds.
- **p50, p99, p99.9**: latency percentiles. For example, 99% of requests finish faster than the p99 value.
- **RSS**: resident set size, the physical memory the process holds.
- **Decay purge**: jemalloc returns unused memory to the operating system after a delay. The profiler reports this work under the function `je_arena_decay`.
- **Spike**: a short period of high latency.
- **perf**: the Linux sampling profiler.
- **NUMA pinning**: binding threads and their memory to one processor socket.

## Test setup

- The host was bench-07: 2 x 32-core Xeon processors, 512 GB memory, Linux kernel 6.8.
- The load average before the runs was 0.4 (nearly idle for 64 cores).
- The workload was ycsb-b with 64 client threads.
- Each build ran 5 times for 10 minutes per run, in alternating order (A, B, A, B, and so on).
- One B run was replaced. The section "Replaced run" gives the reason.

## Results

```
p99 and p99.9 latency, median of 5 runs (1 block = 250 us)

p99    A  █████████  2140 us
       B  ███  870 us   (59% lower)

p99.9  A  ███████████████████████████████████████  9800 us
       B  ████████████  3100 us   (68% lower)
```

Both high-percentile values fell by more than half. Throughput and p50 latency did not move measurably.

Each value is the median of 5 runs. The range in parentheses is the minimum to maximum across those runs.

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change in median | A and B ranges overlap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput (kops/s) | 412 (405 to 418) | 409 (401 to 415) | -3 (-0.7%) | Yes |
| p50 latency (us) | 118 (116 to 121) | 119 (117 to 121) | +1 (+0.8%) | Yes |
| p99 latency (us) | 2140 (1890 to 2610) | 870 (820 to 940) | -1270 (-59.3%) | No |
| p99.9 latency (us) | 9800 (7200 to 14100) | 3100 (2700 to 3900) | -6700 (-68.4%) | No |
| RSS at end of run (GB) | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 (+9.3%) | Range not recorded |

## What the data shows

- **jf2 reduces p99 and p99.9 latency.** The p99 median fell by 1270 us (59.3%). The p99.9 median fell by 6700 us (68.4%) [Ref1].
- **The reduction is larger than the variation between runs.** The slowest B run had a p99 of 940 us. The fastest A run had a p99 of 1890 us [Ref1].
- **B is more consistent between runs.** The p99 range is 120 us wide for B and 720 us wide for A [Ref1].
- **Throughput and p50 latency show no measurable change.** The medians differ by 0.7% and 0.8%. The A and B ranges overlap for both metrics [Ref1].
- **B uses more memory.** RSS at the end of the run was 5.7 GB higher (9.3%) [Ref1].

## Likely cause of the spikes in build A

- The spikes in A occur at the same times as the jemalloc decay purge. The perf profile attributes 31% of the samples taken during spikes to `je_arena_decay` [Ref2].
- Build B runs the purge in a background thread.
- The hypothesis is that purge work on request threads causes the spikes in A. A perf profile of B during its slowest periods would confirm or reject it.

## Replaced run

- Run 3 of B had a 40 s stall at minute 7 of the 10-minute run.
- The stall was traced to logrotate, a nightly scheduled job that rotates log files. The allocator was not the cause [Ref3].
- Run 3 was repeated, and the B results use the repeat.

## Not tested

Insufficient data for these three cases:

- ycsb-a (write-heavy load): the run planned for 2026-11-21 covers this case.
- More than 64 client threads: no run is planned yet.
- NUMA pinning: no run is planned yet.

## Open question

Is the RSS increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%) acceptable? The capacity team must approve it.

## Next steps

1. Run ycsb-a on 2026-11-21.
2. Ask the capacity team to approve the RSS increase.
3. If the capacity team approves, enable jf2 in staging (the pre-production environment), controlled by a configuration flag.

## References

- [Ref1] Benchmark runs of 2026-11-20 on bench-07: ycsb-b, 64 client threads, 5 runs per build, 10 minutes per run.
- [Ref2] perf profile of build A, taken during the spikes in the same runs.
- [Ref3] Investigation of the 40 s stall in run 3 of B, and the repeat of that run.
- [Ref4] YCSB core workload definitions: https://github.com/brianfrankcooper/YCSB/wiki/Core-Workloads

---

Three points to check before you send it:

- **YCSB mixes:** I added the standard read and update percentages from the YCSB documentation. Remove them if the kestrel runs use a custom mix.
- **Cause of the spikes:** I marked it as a hypothesis. Your notes hold a perf profile for A only.
- **RSS:** your notes give one value per build, so the table shows no range.
